title: Chronic Schistosomiasis Presenting with Migrating Pulmonary Manifestation after Recent COVID-19 Infection: HRCT Findings
case_text:
A 38-year-old woman with a Sierra Leonean background presented to our institution complaining of pleural pain, fever, and cough. She had a history of human immunodeficiency virus successfully treated with triple therapy and a recent subclinical COVID-19 infection. The patient had not been to Sierra-Leone for 10 years and there was no history of recent travelling or contact with sick patients or Tuberculosis patients.
Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis with eosinophilia (0.8 10.E9/l) and high CRP (33.7). Further investigation done with a urinary sample, broncho-alveolar lavage, and serological tests (syphilis, hepatitis, Q-fever) concluded negative.
High resolution CT (HRCT) a few days after admission demonstrated multiple nodular zones of consolidation with surrounding ground glass in the left lower lobe (Figure 1A). No TBC-associated lesions or calcified nodes were observed. The first follow-up HRCT was scanned after seven days (Figure 1B) of watchful waiting without any medical therapy. These follow-up images demonstrated a spontaneous regression of some lesions where other nodular lesions demonstrated expansion compared to one week prior. Subsequently the previously described finding of migrating nodular lesions were confirmed on one-month follow-up computed tomography (CT) scan.
The serology was eventually positive for schistosomiasis (IgE 556) and treatment was started (Praziquantel) with an interval of two weeks in between doses. On this therapy the patient improved with significant clinical response and a regression of CRP and eosinophilia.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Schistosomiasis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: chronic pulmonary schistosomiasis presenting with migrating nodular lesions
